extracted.intended_audience: mathematics education researchers, calculus instructors, and graduate students in math education
extracted.subtask_short: analyzing teaching and student understanding in calculus
extracted.subtask_description: Identify and analyze classroom/technology-mediated interactions that reveal how students develop mathematical concepts (e.g., limits, function, eigenvectors), focusing on authority, sociomathematical norms, instrumental genesis, shifts of attention, and representational practices. Use discourse, task-based interviews, and task/interaction analysis to evaluate learner understanding and teaching effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hierarchal authority
rubrics_metrics.description: Hierarchal authority is the authority a person holds because of their position in the class (e.g. as an instructor, or presenter).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When instructors introduce sociomathematical norms, their hierarchal authority can legitimize the expectation before its mathematical meaning is fully interpreted; teachers should be aware of the potentially obstructive role their hierarchical authority may play in negotiation of norms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expertise authority
rubrics_metrics.description: Expertise Authority is legitimized by the perceived expertise of the bearer either by proving their mathematics expertise or by having ownership in the creation of a solution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Instructor or student claims granted by expertise may be accepted prior to full interpretation; be mindful that expertise authority can short-circuit negotiation of meaning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mathematical authority
rubrics_metrics.description: Mathematical authority is legitimized by mathematical argument and justification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mathematical authority plays a role in building a mathematical interpretation, in agreeing on the interpretation, and in validating expectations; when students introduce norms, mathematical argumentation can allow others to interpret and agree on the expectation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Performative authority
rubrics_metrics.description: Performative authority is legitimized by the ability to engage the class.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This form of authority (like others) can be held by instructors or students and contributes to how a claim or expectation gains legitimacy in classroom interaction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criteria for sociomathematical norm adoption
rubrics_metrics.description: For a new expectation to become a sociomathematical norm it needs to be interpreted, agreed upon, and legitimized.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analysis should show how an expectation is (1) interpreted by peers/instructor, (2) negotiated/agreed upon, and (3) legitimized (e.g., via mathematical argument, expertise, or hierarchical endorsement). Note the different consequences when norms are teacher- vs student-initiated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classroom practice: student initiation and negotiation
rubrics_metrics.description: Encourage students rather than the teacher to initiate and negotiate sociomathematical norms to lead to better agreement on expectations among class members.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recommendation: create an environment where student initiation allows mathematical authority to play a validating role; when teachers introduce norms, monitor for possible obstruction from hierarchical/expertise authority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Instrumentalization (tool-directed by user)
rubrics_metrics.description: Instrumentalization: the development of skills to use the tool, personalization and transformation of the tool; what the student thinks the tool was designed for and how the student uses the tool.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assessment should attend to students' evolving uses, personalization of tool use, and the actions/procedures they adopt — evidence of instrumentalization signals that a tool is becoming an instrument for the student.

rubrics_metrics.name: Instrumentation (tool-directed shaping of cognition)
rubrics_metrics.description: Instrumentation: the constraints and potentialities of the tool that shape the student's knowledge acquisition; involves a shift of attention from tool use to what the tool can do so it becomes a mediating instrument.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analysis should identify how the affordances/constraints of a digital tool shape attention and conceptual development (i.e., how the tool 'directs' what students notice and reason about).

rubrics_metrics.name: Using instrumental genesis to detect shifts of attention
rubrics_metrics.description: Analysing processes of instrumentalization reveals evidence of shifts of attention in digital technology environments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for changes in students' actions with the tool (e.g., dragging strategies), the meaning they ascribe to tool outputs, and changes in discourse that indicate shifting focus from tool mechanics to mathematical objects/properties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mason's macro structure of attention
rubrics_metrics.description: At the macro level, attention can vary in multiplicity, locus, focus and sharpness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these macro dimensions to describe broad changes in what and how students attend during an activity (e.g., broad vs narrow focus, shifting locus across representations).

rubrics_metrics.name: Mason's micro states of attending
rubrics_metrics.description: Five micro states of attending: holding wholes; discerning details; recognizing relationships; perceiving properties; reasoning on the basis of agreed properties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify micro-state transitions in student behavior and discourse; note that these states are not strictly ordered and that stable/robust states may block further development of awareness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assessment of student interactions with dynamic geometry environments (DGE)
rubrics_metrics.description: Analyse students' actions with the sketch, different dragging strategies, and their oral communication to evaluate evolving understanding (e.g., of eigenvectors/eigenvalues).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Shifts of attention are made evident by changing focus from the formal definition to the sketch, by specific dragging strategies used to identify eigenvectors, and by how students verbalize and justify observations; document instances where the dragging tool is transformed into an instrument mediating conceptualization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Concept-image vs concept-definition analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: Use Vinner's conceptual model (concept image vs concept definition) to investigate students' understanding of concepts (e.g., function).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Collect responses that reveal students' concept images (common metaphors, typical representations) and compare these to their personal/formal concept definitions to identify mismatches or obstacles to formal understanding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Key features for formal understanding of function
rubrics_metrics.description: Two essential features of the formal concept of function: arbitrariness (domain/range can be arbitrary sets; values at points independent) and univalence (each domain element maps to a unique range element).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether students' concept images support recognition of arbitrariness and univalence; identify common obstacles such as 'having a rule' or 'machine metaphor' that contradict arbitrariness and impede formation of the formal definition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Methodological rubric: task-based interviews and question design
rubrics_metrics.description: Design carefully structured tasks/questions (e.g., graph-identification, existence-of-function, personal-definition prompts) and use task-based interviews to elicit students' concept images and definitions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: the cited study used eight carefully designed questions probing graphs, the possibility of constant functions, and requests for personal definitions; categorize responses according to the chosen conceptual framework.

rubrics_metrics.name: Analyzing teaching of limits via discourse and representational practices
rubrics_metrics.description: Investigate how the limit notation is utilized by instructors and students and how instructor word choice/shifts support students' realizations of limit as process or as a number.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examine instructor discourse for shifts that encourage process-based realizations; watch for frequent emphasis on limit-as-number or overemphasis on dynamic motion which can hinder transition to formal understanding; analyze compatibility among verbal, visual, and symbolic representations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Representational-tool compatibility for limits and calculus concepts
rubrics_metrics.description: Representational tools (verbal, visual, symbolic) used by students/teachers may lead to difficulties if incompatible or if they overemphasize dynamic aspects (e.g., motion) to the detriment of formal understanding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether chosen representations facilitate the transition from intuitive to formal realization; prefer representations and discourse that make formal structure and arbitrariness/limits explicit rather than relying solely on dynamic intuition.
